tier_reason: First-party Bun runs with public benchmark scripts (js-bindings/benchmarks/benchmark-vs-zod.ts, benchmark-vs-all.ts, benchmark-zod4-features.ts) but no CPU model, no Bun version, and the script that wrote docs/benchmarks/benchmark-results.json is not in the repo. The large format/number/coercion ratios are inflated by building the schema inside the timed loop, so the headline claim is overstated; tier stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (release 1.3.1, bun run benchmarks/benchmark-vs-all.ts): 13.8x faster than Zod 4 on the full suite; Number Formats 30-50x, Coercion 23-56x, String Formats 12-27x, ISO 12-22x, Objects 4-7x, Arrays 8x; URL 30.17M/s, 8.0x vs Zod; IPv4 22.28M/s, 1.1x vs Zod. docs/benchmarks/benchmark-results.json (2026-03-18, runtime Bun, 25 rows, average 27.3x): z.email() 6,608,838 vs 416,360 ops/s (15.9x), z.url() 13.8x, z.ipv4() 12.2x, z.int() 54.3x, z.float64() 61.8x, z.coerce.boolean() 74.5x, Object (valid) 4.4x, Nested Object 3.7x, Array<number> 7.8x, Union 1.6x, DiscriminatedUnion 2.1x, Optional 2.2x, Nullable 2.0x. The speedup-all.svg chart shows yet another run (average 29.7x). Rows with schemas built once (objects, arrays, unions, modifiers) are 1.6-7.8x; the 12-75x rows construct a new schema on every iteration.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: TypeScript benchmarks run with Bun (bun run benchmarks/benchmark-vs-all.ts or benchmark-vs-zod.ts; version not stated); Zod ^4.3.6 per js-bindings/package.json devDependencies (benchmark-vs-zod.ts header says Zod 4.3.6); the README's zig build bench -Doptimize=ReleaseFast is the Zig-only benchmark and is not part of the Zod comparison
corrections.workload: Single-value safeParse micro-benchmarks in Bun, 1,000,000 iterations after a 10,000-iteration warm-up, dhi z.* API vs Zod 4: string formats (email, uuid, url, ipv4, jwt, ulid, nanoid, base64), number formats, ISO date/time, coercion, stringbool, a 3-field object, a nested object, Array<number> of 10, unions and optional/nullable. In benchmark-zod4-features.ts the format, number and coercion rows build the schema inside the timed closure (e.g. zod.email().safeParse(...)), so they time schema construction plus one parse.
corrections.caveats: First-party; CPU, Bun version and the script that produced benchmark-results.json are not published (none of the four js-bindings benchmark scripts writes that file). The 12-75x rows build a fresh schema per iteration in the timed loop, which mostly measures Zod 4's expensive schema construction (Zod runs about 0.3-0.5M ops/s on those rows but 1.9M ops/s on a hoisted 3-field object that includes an email check); rows with hoisted schemas show 1.6-7.8x, and the README's own 1.3.1 table has IPv4 at only 1.1x. Despite the 'SIMD WASM' description, the TypeScript path is mostly plain JavaScript: v1.1.20 called WASM only for url, ipv4 and ISO datetime, v1.5.2 only for ISO datetime, and since v1.6.0 (2026-08-30) the default entry is a single runtime-agnostic TypeScript core with no WASM dependency, so the measured gain is a faster JS reimplementation (JIT-compiled validators), not Zig/WASM. Runs on Bun (JavaScriptCore), not V8. Three different summary figures (13.8x README, 27.3x JSON, 29.7x chart) come from different runs.

notes: Numbers in the record match benchmark-results.json and the README, but the big ratios come from per-iteration schema construction in the timed loop; hoisted-schema rows are 1.6-7.8x. The TypeScript speedup is from a pure-JS core (WASM was used only for url/ipv4/datetime early on and not at all since v1.6.0), so the assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs category is a weak fit; consider a category override to a JS/TS validation category or keep with that shortcoming. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 387 stars, 6 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-31 (v1.7.0).

tier_reason: First-party README table against the md5 npm package on an unnamed 'slow production server' with Node v10.18.1; no CPU model and no benchmark script in the repo, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '30x faster than the most popular md5 utility' (md5 npm). Table (Node v10.18.1, Ubuntu): 37 MB 38,500 ms vs 990 ms (0.96 vs 37 MB/s), about 39x (derived from page data); 24 MB 23,600 vs 700 ms; 12 MB 12,400 vs 490 ms; 8 MB 7,600 vs 400 ms; 4 MB 4,000 vs 330 ms; 2 MB 2,000 vs 240 ms; 1 MB 1,000 vs 170 ms; 0.5 MB 520 vs 360 ms; 0.3 MB 390 vs 300 ms; 0.2 MB 260 vs 90 ms
corrections.caveats: First-party table from an unnamed 'slow production server', Node v10.18.1 (2019-era V8), no CPU model and no public benchmark script. The baseline md5 npm package runs at about 1 MB/s and is not a tuned JavaScript MD5; Node's built-in crypto.createHash('md5') (native OpenSSL), the obvious server-side incumbent, is not compared. In the current md5-wasm.js only inputs larger than 1,048,576 bytes (bounder) go to WebAssembly; smaller inputs use the bundled pure-JS MD5, so the 0.2-1 MB rows compare two JavaScript implementations, and the WASM path instantiates a new module on every call (about 150 ms per the README) and finishes the tail in JS. The README itself expected 3-5x and attributes the larger gap to number-format conversions in the md5 package. Code dates from 2020-2021; the 2026-04-23 commit ('Fighting with git') is housekeeping.

notes: README table and 30x claim verified; derived 39x at 37 MB is correct. Metadata confirmed: MIT (LICENSE.md, package.json), 34 stars, 3 forks, 25 commits, last commit 2026-04-23, so active by the 12-month rule although the code is essentially from 2021. Main shortcomings for the record: weak baseline (slow md5 npm, Node crypto not compared), no hardware or script, small-file rows run the JS fallback.

tier_reason: The ultrachess WASM side is reproducible (rust/bench/wasm-perft.mjs, rustc 1.95.0, release LTO fat, codegen-units 1, Apple M4 Max, Node 25.7.0, Bun 1.3.10), but the chess.js baseline is a cited 5-7 Mnps figure that the repo never measures and whose upstream source is not linked (the chess.js README has no perft numbers), so the comparison is cross-run at best: C.

corrections.caveats: The chess.js (5-7 Mnps, 'Node 22') and chessops (2-3 Mnps) figures are cited without a source link and were never run in the project's harness, although chess.js is already a devDependency (used for differential fuzzing); the chess.js README has no perft numbers. The 55x/95x ratios are therefore cross-run comparisons on unknown hardware. BENCH.md caveat 6: ultrachess perft bulk-counts at depth 1 (popcount of target bitboards instead of materialising moves), while chess.js perft makes and unmakes every leaf move, so perft overstates the gap for real move-by-move use. Perft is a move-generation microbenchmark and says nothing about PGN/SAN parsing or full-library workloads. Single machine (Apple M4 Max), min of 3 trials. Young repo (43 commits, all in April 2026; latest 2026-04-18).

notes: Numbers in the record match BENCH.md and the README (Bun 204.9 ms / 581.0 Mnps, Node 353.7 ms / 336.7 Mnps, chess.js 5-7 Mnps cited, ~55x Node, ~95x Bun, ~140x native). Metadata confirmed: MIT, 7 stars, 2 forks, not a fork, npm package ultrachess 1.4.0, last commit 2026-04-18. The same BENCH.md carries same-harness native-Rust perft vs shakmaty 0.30, cozy-chess 0.3.4 and chess 3.2.0 (rust/bench/src/bin/nps.rs, geomean 3.70x shakmaty, 1.23x cozy) that would qualify as tier A for a Rust-library entry, but that is not this record's baseline; under the cross-run precedent (PostgreSQL, MySQL, ODB) the orchestrator may prefer D for the chess.js claim.
